title: Resilience has a cost. So does complacency.
gist: Amid drone and missile attacks and a Strait of Hormuz closure, the author argues GCC states should buy 'calibrated' rather than maximum resilience, using the operations-research critical fractile (Cu/(Cu+Co)) to set redundancy standards sector by sector. Real resilience requires avoiding common points of failure, a six-country GCC resilience commission to deepen interoperability, and investment in human capital.

insights.claim: The cost of resilience is concrete — spare industrial capacity, inventories, alternative supply chains, redundancy — while the cost of complacency stays abstract and is therefore underweighted, though it can be much larger if something goes wrong.
insights.so_what: Expect Gulf governments to reallocate capital toward redundancy and stockpiles after recent attacks.
insights.quote: The cost of complacency stays abstract, and so it tends to be underweighted.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The critical fractile from operations research sets optimal coverage as Cu/(Cu+Co); if a shortfall costs nine times as much as a surplus, optimal coverage is 90 percent.
insights.so_what: Provides a quantitative rule for sizing redundancy in critical infrastructure.
insights.quote: If a shortfall costs nine times as much as a surplus, the optimal coverage is 90 percent.
insights.locator: One useful tool to analyze this challenge
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: GCC governments should set resilience standards sector by sector according to the consequences of failure — e.g., water, power and hospitals warrant more redundancy than hotels — rather than one standard across the economy.
insights.so_what: Points to targeted capex in utilities, desalination and health systems.
insights.quote: The goal is calibrated resilience, not maximum resilience.
insights.locator: One useful tool to analyze this challenge
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: More capacity does not automatically mean more resilience: a second desalination plant on the same grid or two pipelines through the same vulnerable corridor offer only nominal redundancy; the key is avoiding common points of failure, including shared software, networks or specialist teams.
insights.so_what: Investment should favor genuinely diversified routes and systems, not duplicated assets.
insights.quote: Two pipelines provide only nominal redundancy if they pass through the same vulnerable corridor.
insights.locator: More capacity does not automatically mean
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The longstanding criticism that plans like Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 deployed capital without enough attention to value creation still holds, but spare capacity that once looked like waste may now be a sensible insurance premium.
insights.so_what: Reframes some Gulf overbuild as strategic insurance — changes how investors should judge return-on-capital critiques.
insights.quote: spare capacity that once looked like waste may now be a sensible insurance premium
insights.locator: One should think of redundancy as optionality
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: The GCC should set up a six-country joint resilience commission to build infrastructure resilience, with cross-border linkages more important than redundant national networks.
insights.so_what: Could drive cross-border grid, pipeline and logistics projects across the Gulf.
insights.quote: The sum of GCC resilience is greater than its individual parts.

insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: When the Strait of Hormuz was first shut, GCC states supported one another to bring hydrocarbon product to market, showing the value of interoperability given the Arabian peninsula's chokepoints.
insights.so_what: Intra-GCC export rerouting mitigates but does not eliminate chokepoint risk to oil flows.
insights.locator: As a first step, the GCC should
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council

insights.claim: Since no plan can cover every disruption, investment in human capital — people able to adapt and improvise — is perhaps the most important resilience investment, as drilling on a nuclear submarine and civilian endurance in Ukraine illustrate.
insights.so_what: Supports Gulf spending on training and workforce readiness alongside physical hardening.
insights.quote: When the plans run out, resilience depends on people who can adapt and improvise.
insights.locator: People are the most important part
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
